subject: Archaeology
title: What Romans Ate: Trash Tells the Truth
description: A quick win: understand What Romans Ate: Trash Tells the Truth.

hook.text: The best way to understand Roman life is to dig through their garbage. Trash does not lie.

buildup.text: Monte Testaccio in Rome is a hill made entirely of 53 million broken olive oil jars — ancient industrial waste.

discovery.text: The jars came from Spain and North Africa. Stamps on them reveal shippers, dates, and trade routes spanning centuries.

twist.text: Romans ate flamingo tongues, dormice fattened in jars, and garum — a fermented fish sauce they put on everything.

climax.text: Sewer analysis at Herculaneum shows the poor ate well: eggs, fish, figs, olives, and chicken were all common.

punchline.text: Roman sewers proved that even the poor ate better than expected.

quiz.question: What is Monte Testaccio in Rome?
options: A natural hill where Rome's first settlers lived
A hill made entirely of 53 million broken olive oil jars
The largest Roman cemetery, containing over a million burials

details.summary: Analysis of Roman rubbish dumps, sewers, and cesspits reveals a diet far more varied than literary sources suggest. Ordinary Romans ate wheat bread, lentils, olives, figs, pork, fish, and garum (fermented fish sauce), with diets varying significantly by class, region, and proximity to trade routes.
details.whyItMatters: Food waste is honest evidence — people throw away what they actually eat, not what they aspire to eat. Archaeological diet evidence corrects literary biases and reveals the true nutrition of all social classes, not just elites.
takeaways: Roman diets are reconstructed from trash dumps and sewer deposits
Ordinary Romans ate bread, lentils, olives, pork, and fish sauce
Diet varied significantly by class, region, and trade access

faq.question: What was garum and why was it everywhere?
faq.answer: Garum was a fermented fish sauce made by salting fish intestines and leaving them to break down in the sun for months. Romans used it like modern soy sauce or ketchup — on almost everything. Production facilities have been found across the Mediterranean, and amphorae prove massive trade volumes.

faq.question: How do archaeologists analyze ancient diets?
faq.answer: Through animal bones, plant seeds, and pollen in deposits; chemical analysis of residues on cooking pots; isotope analysis of human bones showing protein sources; and parasite eggs in sewage revealing digestive health. Together these methods reconstruct diets with surprising precision.
